CHIEF COMPLAINT
Chest pain, referred from emergency room for evaluation of possible esophagitis.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a new patient who initially presented to the emergency room in early October 2020 with four days of chest pain. The pain was located in the center of her chest behind the breastbone, described as sharp and felt like a heart attack. The pain occurred randomly without a clear trigger and did not improve with any self-measures. Patient notes the pain was worse with eating. She also experienced difficulty swallowing during this time. She presented to the emergency room on day four of her symptoms. Workup in the ER included EKG and blood tests, which were all normal, and cardiac workup was normal. She was referred to our clinic for possible GI etiology. Pain and swallowing difficulty resolved approximately three days after the ER visit. Patient has been asymptomatic for three months but reports feeling like something is wrong. During the time of symptom onset, patient was experiencing stress related to a job transition. Denies current abdominal pain, and reports normal bowel movements. Patient has been trying to lose weight.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies current chest pain, dysphagia, or abdominal pain. Bowel movements normal. Denies family history of gastrointestinal problems.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Uterine fibroids, anemia, cholecystectomy (several years ago).

MEDICATIONS
Not documented.

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
No known family history of gastrointestinal problems.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Recent job transition associated with significant stress. Currently attempting weight loss.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: Lower abdomen soft without pain or tenderness. Upper abdominal quadrants with mild tenderness to light palpation, symmetric. No rebound or guarding. Otherwise, exam normal.

RESULTS
ER EKG: normal. ER blood tests: normal. Cardiac workup: normal.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
58-year-old female with history of four-day episode of chest pain and dysphagia in October 2020, now resolved. Differential diagnosis includes GERD, dyspepsia, esophagitis, musculoskeletal etiologies, and anxiety. Most likely etiology is anxiety-related chest pain in setting of job transition, with possible musculoskeletal component. Given that patient has been asymptomatic for three months, if esophagitis were present, it would likely have already healed and would not be visualized on endoscopy. Discussed option of EGD versus observation and symptomatic monitoring. Patient elected to defer EGD and self-monitor for any recurrent symptoms. Patient instructed to call office if any additional episodes of pain or concerning symptoms occur, at which time EGD can be scheduled. Will follow up as needed for any other gastrointestinal complaints.
